content.p: For two days in August 2018, a Colorado father stood on his front porch and told television crews that he wanted his wife and daughters back. Christopher Watts, 33, said the house felt empty. On the third day he was in custody, and by the end of that week the bodies of Shanann Watts, 34, who was 15 weeks pregnant, and of her daughters Bella, 4, and Celeste, 3, had been recovered from an oil company's work site near Frederick, Colorado.

Watts pleaded guilty on 6 November 2018 to all nine charges against him. On 19 November a Weld County judge sentenced him to five life terms without the possibility of parole, plus further years, in a plea agreement that removed the death penalty. He remains in prison.

Shanann Watts posted often about her husband, whom she married in 2012 and called her "rock". Friends and colleagues described a happy household, and a co-worker at the nutrition-supplement company where Shanann worked as a brand promoter said she had seemed upbeat at a leadership seminar in Scottsdale, Arizona, the weekend before she vanished.

Money was tighter than the posts suggested. A June 2015 bankruptcy filing, reported by CBS News, listed about $70,000 in unsecured claims on top of a sizeable mortgage, from credit cards, student loans and medical bills. At the time of the killings Watts worked as an operator for Anadarko Petroleum, which CBS said paid him about $61,500 a year. NBC News reported that the 2015 filing showed less than $10 in each of two savings accounts.

Prosecutors later said that the pictures of a smiling family hid something else. During the summer, while Shanann and the girls spent time with her parents in North Carolina, Watts began seeing a co-worker. Rourke told the sentencing court that Watts had searched for secluded vacation spots and had talked to a real estate agent about selling the family home. He said Watts did not take an interest in the self-help books his wife gave him. Shanann, Rourke said, had noticed credit-card alerts for restaurant spending in north Denver while she was in North Carolina, and had confronted him more than once.

Shanann flew home from the Arizona trip and was dropped at the house by a friend, Nickole Atkinson, at about 2 a.m., according to the friend's account on ABC's "Good Morning America" reported by NBC News. Atkinson said Shanann was not feeling well. When Shanann missed a 10 a.m. doctor's appointment and stopped answering calls and texts, Atkinson went to the house, found Shanann's car with both car seats still inside, and asked police to check on the family. A Frederick officer arrived shortly before 2 p.m., KOAA reported.

Watts agreed to let the officer in. Inside, police found Shanann's purse, phone, wallet and medication, according to the arrest affidavit as summarised by CNN, but not the three people. Watts told police that he had woken that morning and told his wife he wanted a separation, that the two were upset and crying but had not argued, and that he had left for work. A neighbour's security video confirmed his departure at about 5:27 a.m., NBC News reported the affidavit as saying. The local police soon asked for help, and the Colorado Bureau of Investigation and the FBI joined the search.

Watts spoke to Denver's KMGH from the porch. "I just want everybody to come home," he said (NBC News quotes it as "everybody to just come home"), and described an "emotional conversation" with his wife that he would not elaborate on. Some viewers and investigators noticed how restrained he seemed, PEOPLE reported.

Within a day, investigators had learned that Watts was involved with a co-worker, which he had denied in earlier interviews, according to the affidavit. Nichol Kessinger, who told The Denver Post she met him through her work for a petroleum contractor, said she called police on 15 August after concluding that he was lying to her. He had told her he was nearly divorced. Rourke later said she was "absolutely instrumental" in the investigation. The affidavit did not name the co-worker it referred to, and CNN noted it was not clear whether that was Kessinger.

According to the affidavit, Watts said he would tell "the truth" if he could speak to his father. He then said that after the talk about separating he had looked at a baby monitor and seen Bella lying blue on her bed and Shanann strangling Celeste, and that he had gone into a rage and strangled Shanann. He told officers he put all three bodies in his work truck, buried Shanann near some tanks at an oil work site and put the girls in the tanks. He pointed out the three locations. The affidavit also records that, before the confession, a drone search had spotted a bedsheet in the field that matched bedding found in the trash at the Watts home, and what officers called fresh movement of dirt consistent with a clandestine grave.

Shanann's body was found on Thursday 16 August in a shallow grave on Anadarko property, and the girls' bodies were in oil tanks nearby, according to a prosecution filing quoted by CNN. Colorado Bureau of Investigation director John Camper told a news conference that investigators were working to establish exactly what had happened. Anadarko said Watts no longer worked there and that the company was heartbroken. A prosecutor told the court that investigators believed the family had been killed at the house.

On Monday 20 August the Weld County District Attorney's Office charged Watts with nine felonies. Three were first-degree murder counts, and two more accused him of killing a child under 12 while in a position of trust. A further count concerned the unlawful ending of the pregnancy, and the last three concerned tampering with a body. Defence attorneys filed motions asking for swabs of the girls' necks and throats and for their own DNA expert to attend the autopsies. Judge Kopcow denied them, saying "The court cannot order the prosecution and/or coroner how to conduct their investigation."

On Tuesday 6 November, Watts pleaded guilty to the nine charges. Rourke told reporters that he had flown to North Carolina some weeks earlier to discuss a deal with Shanann's relatives and that they agreed to take the death penalty off the table. He said he was not willing to offer any other concession, and that investigators had never believed the account in the affidavit. Shanann's mother, father and brother were in court but did not speak to the media.

NBC News counted the pleas as five murder counts, three counts of tampering and one count over the pregnancy. At the sentencing hearing, Rourke told the court that Watts's version, in which he killed Shanann in an uncontrolled rage, was not true, and that Watts had killed her deliberately and then suffocated the girls. These are the prosecutor's statements to the court, not findings from a trial, because there was no trial.
The hearing took place in Greeley. Friends of Shanann and neighbours from the family's subdivision lined up in the courthouse, and an overflow room was opened for people watching a video stream.

Frank Rzucek, Shanann's father, spoke first. "I trusted you to take care of them, not kill them," he told Watts. "You heartless monster." Her brother, Frank Rzucek Jr., had Rourke read a statement that said "What kind of person slaughters the people they love the most?" His mother, Sandra Rzucek, said: "I didn't want death for you because that's not my right. Your life is between you and God." The family had told the prosecutor they did not want the death penalty because nobody has the right to take another life.

Watts's parents, Cindy and Ronnie Watts, also addressed the court. Earlier they had defended their son and questioned the plea deal in a KMGH interview, but in court they read a prepared statement saying the killings should never have happened. "We love you," Cindy Watts said to her son, "and we forgive you, son."

Watts himself said only "No, sir" when asked whether he wanted to make a statement. One of his attorneys told the court he was "sincerely sorry". Judge Kopcow called the killings "the most inhumane and vicious crime that I have handled out of the thousands of cases that I have seen."

The sentence was five life terms without parole, three to run consecutively and two concurrently, the first three for the deaths of Shanann, Bella and Celeste. He received 48 years for the unlawful termination of the pregnancy and 36 years for tampering with the bodies. NBC News reported that those terms run consecutively to the three consecutive life terms. Rourke said afterwards that he doubted Watts would ever give an honest account of why he did it, and that Watts's research for secluded vacation spots showed he had found a new love interest. Prosecutors later said they believed his wish for a fresh start was a motive. In the courtroom he had said that "in his mind divorce wasn't an option".

On the day of sentencing, Shanann's parents filed a wrongful death suit against Watts seeking more than $100,000, Oxygen reported, citing KDVR. The filing accused him of trying to mislead investigators.

Days after the sentencing, Colorado authorities released footage from a neighbour's security camera from the early hours of 13 August that showed Watts loading a gas can into his truck and backing it into his garage. PEOPLE reported that prosecutors thought he then put the bodies in the truck. The Colorado Department of Corrections said in early December that Watts had been moved out of state for safety reasons, which it said can happen to high-profile prisoners under an interstate compact. Wisconsin's corrections department would not confirm his location in 2018. A 2026 report from Fox News Digital, carried by FOX6 Milwaukee, put him at Dodge Correctional Institution, a maximum-security prison in Waupun, Wisconsin, and said People had reported that he and a woman had applied to marry within the prison system. Fox News Digital said it had asked the Wisconsin Department of Corrections for comment.
Sources differ on where the family lived. The Associated Press, in a December 2018 report, placed the home in Firestone, while most reports, including CNN's, describe Frederick.
